newsitem.title: UK: Med crude markets firm quietly on Iraq absence.
newsitem.headline: Med crude markets firm quietly on Iraq absence.

text.p: Mediterranean oil markets were quiet but firm on Monday, with the absence of Iraqi barrels in July buoying Urals prices, traders said.

News of further delays to Iraqi exports did not rouse a violent response, with players saying the market had already doubted the early July target date given last week by Iraq's oil minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed.
"It doesn't surprise me, nobody really believed the target anyway," said one buyer of Russian Urals, the alternative Mediterranean sour crude.
"For July it's a Urals market only and basically people are short, the situation is tight," he added.
Iraqi envoy Abdul Amir al-Anbari said at the weekend he did not anticipate Baghdad restarting crude flows until August under the second term of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
But the news did help Urals to lift further, with a major offering a July 12-13 Urals loader for dated Brent -60 cents and talking of bids last Friday at -65 cents.
"The situation is worsening, every day that goes by makes things worse, so people will have to pay up," the seller said.
A Spanish refiner was heard to have bought fob Urals barrels last Thursday for a price equivalent to around 70 cents a barrel below dated Brent.
Most Urals for first half July was believed already committed to end-users and there was a suggestion buyers were holding back until the supply situation for second half July clarifies.
Sweet markets were more balanced, though poor refining margins threatened to bring about run cuts that would stifle demand, one trader said.
Some West African barrels have already been bought to supply the Med in July but demand was thought sporadic.
Prices were largely steady. A major bought a third decade Bonny Light on Friday at between 45 and 50 cents a barrel above dated Brent and a Qua Iboe was also on offer.
"There is not such strong demand for sweet crude in the Med. People are staring at negative margins and will cut sweet runs first," said one trader.
However, rumours circulated that two Syrian light cargoes were traded on Friday at a double digit premium to the official selling price of 55 cents a barrel below dated Brent.
Yet Algeria's Sonatrach was believed struggling to find buyers willing to pay the premium it wanted over its OSP of 40 cents above benchmark Dated Brent.
